meta.title: Hungarian Phrases and Expressions
meta.subtitle: 542 expressions · 87 everyday, 387 idioms, 68 proverbs · both directions
meta.desc: 542 Hungarian set phrases, idioms and proverbs, in three subdecks: 87 everyday phrases, 387 idioms and 68 proverbs. Both study directions come as two cards of one expression — Hungarian → English (see the Hungarian, recall the meaning) and English → Hungarian (see an English meaning, recall the Hungarian) — each with a schedule of its own. This is a companion to the five level decks, Hungarian A1 to C1, and not one of them: a level is a list of words, and an expression is a unit a list of words cannot see. Nothing here is taught by any of the five, so the two can be studied together without repeating an entry. The PHRASES are the expressions Wiktionary files as phrases or interjections and does not mark as idiomatic — mostly the everyday formulas a Hungarian speaker uses as one piece (nem tudom, még mindig, nem értem …). The IDIOMS are expressions whose meaning is not their words' (szüksége van, igaza van, igazat mond …), most of them verbs, given like every verb on the shelf in the third person singular; and the PROVERBS the sayings Wiktionary files as proverbs (az idő pénz, tévedni emberi dolog, hallgatni arany …), each glossed with the English proverb that says the same where there is one. Within each subdeck the expressions come in the order of how many of Tatoeba's Hungarian sentences contain them, an idiom that is a verb being counted with its verb in any form and in either order; only 271 of the 542 are found there at all, and the rest follow in the order of how common their rarest word is in film and television subtitles. Real example sentences come with 270 of the 542 expressions, three apiece for 124, with the expression picked out in colour and a speaker beside the sentence and the headword. Sources. Expressions, meanings and the idiom and proverb labels: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Order: Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR, then a word list built from OpenSubtitles (hermitdave/FrequencyWords, CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: Tatoeba, CC BY 2.0 FR.
